scores.evidence: Eventual convergence (AP) using a CRDT. Edits apply locally and merge later, so editing survives disconnects.
scores.rationale: Yjs, state-vector resync, server-side ack-after-commit, and E2EE conflict are stated accurately; minor imprecision (consistent-hash 'single writer', 'should be 0' RPO vs 5s, no tombstone/GC detail) remains.

scores.evidence: Adopt open-source Yjs, self-hosted. Do not write a CRDT.
scores.rationale: Covers core capabilities with explicit deferrals (comments, version history UI, offline mobile), but rich-text merge semantics and version history are deferred or thin.

scores.evidence: One codebase, two runtime processes: a stateless API (auth, metadata, sharing) and a stateful sync gateway (WebSocket).
scores.rationale: Responsibilities and data ownership are clear; minor loose ends: the '≤3 deployables (web, API, sync)' versus two processes, and async snapshot workers not counted.

scores.evidence: 0 lost acknowledged edits over 1,000 kill trials; restored state byte-identical; revoked user is disconnected within 5 s (ASSUMPTION)
scores.rationale: Validation is tied to specific risks, done early (V1 spike before commitment), with checkable labeled thresholds and post-launch SLO-gated staged exposure.

scores.evidence: Missing inputs: Data classification and compliance regimes... Needed before V2; they could change the tenancy and residency rows.
scores.rationale: Assumptions are labeled, missing inputs are named with owners and deadlines, and revisit triggers say what would change.

scores.evidence: Paste and import sanitization (XSS); Fails closed; connection and size caps
scores.rationale: Covers crash/durability, revocation, cross-tenant, abuse limits and chaos, but malicious Yjs update validation, tombstone bloat and poison-update handling are not explicit.

scores.evidence: deploys to production behind a feature flag, with a one-command rollback to the previous image.
scores.rationale: Deploy, rollback, dashboards, SLO alerts and runbooks are present; incident ownership and rolling-deploy protocol compatibility are thinner.

scores.evidence: Infrastructure cost | Cost per active doc-hour | UNKNOWN (missing input: budget ceiling
scores.rationale: Cost is measured and gated and build vs buy is noted, but there is no analysis of cost drivers (memory per hot doc, websocket connections, log storage) or growth.

scores.evidence: R3 (data gravity: every stored doc is in the library's format)
scores.rationale: Reversibility classes are assigned to each decision, R3 decisions are validated first by V1 and frozen, and flip triggers and compaction point of no return are explicit.

scores.evidence: ≤ 3 deployables (web, API, sync) plus Postgres and one object store
scores.rationale: Mostly proportionate with a monolith and a single Postgres; some ceremony (penetration test, Kubernetes/ECS, dense validation IDs) is heavy but justified by confidentiality.

scores.evidence: Run the V1 spike: convergence, encoding, schema versioning, and size. Freeze the document schema, ID scheme, update-log format
scores.rationale: Build order is justified by dependencies and risk, with concrete tasks, exit checks, evidence locations and failure fallbacks.

checklist.evidence: Adopt open-source Yjs, self-hosted. Do not write a CRDT.
Freeze the document schema, ID scheme, update-log format, and sync protocol with version fields.
5 simulated clients, 10k random edits with network partitions and reordering
The server acknowledges an edit only after it is committed to the log (group commit, 50 ms batches).
Consistent-hash routing so every editor of a doc hits the same sync node (single writer per doc).
Re-check permissions on role changes and revocation, by disconnecting live sessions.
Add presence and cursors (ephemeral, never persisted).
Phase 0 two users type; Phase 1 V1 spike; Phase 2 durability; Phase 4 features
500k characters, 2 MB encoded state; Load test with 50 editors on a doc

traps.evidence: Phase 0: Two allow-listed internal users open the same document... User B sees it.
The server acknowledges an edit only after it is committed to the log
End-to-end encryption... would conflict with server-side merging

note: Strong, risk-ordered plan that adopts Yjs and validates it early with durability and authz gates; weaker on rich-text merge semantics, undo and version history detail, large-doc memory and cost drivers.
